To the first point, refrigeration can definitely slow an infection but it may not stop it from growing altogether.

As far as refrigerating certain types of stouts, that's going to be totally up to the individual. Spices, coffee, and alcohol content can fade with time, especially at warmer temperatures. If you drink a beverage and think it's at the perfect spot for you, then store any others you have in the refrigerator to slow any changes. Again, this will slow but not stop the beverage from changing. However, if you try one and it doesn't seem quite where you want it (too much coffee, too boozy, too much pepper heat), then store it warmer to allow the changes to take place a bit quicker. Cellar temperature is preferred (~55F), but if you can't do that, then just put it in the coolest and darkest place you can.

It's interesting to see how changes happen over time. Some beverages lose all their magic, and others become phenomenal. I had a certain vintage about 6 months ago and it was perfect, but I also had another one around the same time and it was a shadow of its former self.

I first place the aged beverages in a cooling chamber until they reach 40-55F, depending on the specific product I'm testing. Once the optimal temperature is reached, I remove the containers from the cooling chamber and using a small pry bar, I remove the seal; some containers may require the use of a pointed, spiral tool for this step.

At this stage, certain samples may react with the environment and self-decant. In this case, it is usually an indicator of bacterial infection; however, if a sample is salvageable, I will usually continue to the next steps of the testing process.

This part can be tricky, so make sure to wear your lab coat and goggles, then carefully decant some of the sample into a glass receptacle. Avoid using plastic as this can negatively impact the sample. Once an acceptable sample size has been decanted into your receptacle, observe the sample and note any irregular foaming and look for the presence of debris in the sample. Carefully test the aroma of the sample and note any unpleasantness.

Finally, and this is important, gently raise the receptacle and pour a small quantity into your mouth. Note the taste and texture and whether or not both are appropriate for the sample you are testing. If anything unpleasant is noticed, discard the sample and repeat the test with 10 or 12 others.

I've been in sales for 15 years, I organize events with various organizations and individuals, and I host a radio show where I interview guests. I have to be on the phone or behind a mic a lot. So here's my advice based on my experience.

* Relax - This is key. I'm sure you're thinking, "Sure, if I could do that I'd be fine!", so let me give you some tips to help with this one...
* Be prepared - There's no way that you'll know everything about your job, and it's OK if others are more knowledgeable than you. Just be as prepared as you can be as it pertains to your job. Strive to learn more and be a better you each day.
* Things won't always go to script - Have your script or bullet points ready but be prepared to deviate from that. For example, if a customer asks you a question that's not on your script it's OK to say, "Could you give me just a moment to find this information for you?" Then when you find that out you'll have that piece of information ready for next time someone asks. Over time you'll build up your knowledge.
* It's OK to not know something - Reiterating what I said above. You can't know everything about everything, but you can learn. If a customer asks you a question and you can look it up quickly then ask them politely to give you a moment to do so. If it may take a little longer for you to get the information say something like, "I apologize but I don't have that information available right now. Would it be OK if I research this and get back with you?"
* Be courteous - This is a simple one but very important. If you are courteous when dealing with people they'll be much more relaxed in dealing with you, making it much easier for you to speak with them.
* Be ready for angry customers - I'm not sure what industry you're in but most sectors with phone support will occasionally have angry customers. Just remember the points above and try not to lose your cool. If you're calm and respectful with someone, and let them know you understand their frustration, you can usually work things out.
* Don't overthink things - I can tell from your post that you're working yourself up over "what if" situations. That will drive you insane and make any task more difficult if you're worried about every scenario that could go wrong. Things will go wrong, you'll stumble over your words, you won't have some info ready, a customer will get upset... and all of that is OK. Don't stress yourself out thinking about what might go wrong.

Good luck. Making or receiving phone calls can be stressful, but with some planning and a good attitude it gets better.

Referring to the session IPA and session pale ale, it's really a grey area and likely comes down to whatever the brewery decides to call it. IBU and hop character could play into it, but there really is no clear cut line between session pale ale and IPA.

This is a big generalization, but for pale ale, IPA, and double IPA... pale ale will have noticeable hop presence but balanced with the maltiness, ABV will typically be around 6% or lower. IPA will have a more assertive hop presence and bitterness plus higher ABV, but less than 7.5%, with balance being definitely hop-forward. Double IPA is going to be very assertive on the hop profile and can have a heavier malt presence, with ABV above 7.5%.

However, you get into specialty styles of each of these and it blurs the lines even more, like with what people consider West Coast IPA or New England IPA.

accessibility to beer ≠ accessibility to good beer

Breweries per capita is a good number to look at when analyzing economics, but not a quality beer city. In my experience, a state with looser beer laws where it's easier to open a brewery tends to have more mediocre to poor quality beer. States with tougher restrictions mean only (or mostly) those really dedicated to the craft choose to open.

Active brewery permits aren't really relevant, as the ones that aren't included in the per capita numbers (breweries-in-planning?) don't have any track record to show if they make quality beer.

Home price is meaningless for these purposes; walkability is a good metric to look at when judging a beer town. It's always nice to be able to get to several breweries/bars without the need to drive or catch a ride.

There's no mention at all of the quality/ratings of the beer in each city. I've visited places with a few really good breweries and places with a ton of mediocre breweries; I'll choose the location with a smaller number of good breweries every time. No offense to certain cities, but I don't hear anyone raving about taking a beer trip there, same goes for others with similar reputations.
